You need to find all error messages in a 10,000-line log file. Or extract usernames from system files. Or count how many times a specific IP address appears in access logs.
Opening the file in an editor and searching manually? That's slow and error-prone.
Linux text processing tools turn these tasks into one-line commands.
cut extracts specific characters or fields from each line.
# Get first character from each line
cut -c1 file.txt

# Get characters 1-3
cut -c1-3 file.txt

# Get characters 1, 2, and 4
cut -c1,2,4 file.txt

ls -l | cut -c1-10
# Output: drwxr-xr-x, -rw-r--r--, etc.

awk is powerful for extracting and manipulating fields (columns).

articles.description:
After 25 years in industrial maintenance, I shipped my first mobile app. Here's the technical breakdown.
Flutter - Single codebase for Android (iOS coming)
Firebase - Auth, Firestore, Cloud Storage
Claude Code - AI-assisted development and debugging
Most "digital business card" apps just generate QR codes. I wanted real NFC tap-to-share, like Google Pay but for contact info.
Android's Host Card Emulation (HCE) lets your phone act as an NFC card. The tricky part: implementing NDEF message handling properly.
Flutter doesn't have great HCE packages, so I had to write platform channels to handle the native Android side.
As a solo developer, Claude Code was a game-changer:
Multi-file refactoring without losing context
Debugging NFC edge cases methodically
Writing Firebase security rules correctly the first time
I also tested Gemini Pro 3 - excellent for reasoning through architecture decisions, but Claude Code was more reliable for actual implementation.
Start with Firebase - Zero backend setup, ship faster
Flutter hot reload - Iteration speed is insane
HCE is underused - Most devs don't know Android phones can emulate NFC cards natively
👉 https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.cardscontrol.app
Questions about the implementation? Ask in the comments.
articles.title: How I Built a Digital Business Card App with Flutter, HCE, and Claude Code

articles.description:
One of the biggest misunderstandings about AI — especially among beginners — is the idea that it thinks.
It doesn’t.
This might sound like a technical or philosophical distinction, but in practice it causes very real problems in how people use and trust AI systems.
What people usually mean by “AI thinks”
When someone says an AI is thinking, they often mean that it:
understands what it’s saying
knows whether something is true
reasons about the world like a human would
Modern AI systems do none of these things.
They don’t have beliefs, intentions, or awareness. They don’t know when they’re wrong.
What they do instead is much simpler — and more limited.
What AI is actually doing
Most modern AI systems are pattern recognisers and predictors.
At a high level, they:
analyse large amounts of data…
